rv.q: A hugely entertaining blast of unadorned nostalgia

Add to this some extremely impressive performances, notably from Adam Jackson-Smith as Fawlty. He’s not just some tall, skinny chap with a ’tache. He embodies the character both vocally, with an uncanny likeness to Cleese, and physically - all bendy rubberiness - and captures the splenetic outbursts, the waspish asides and inner pain.

But as shamelessly recycled 50-year-old comic material goes, John Cleese and Connie Booth’s stage replica of their classic TV comedy, Fawlty Towers, is still very good fun. It’s such a high-quality copy of the 1975 original that if you look closely, you might even find it says ‘Made In China’ on the bottom.

Fawlty Towers The Play will, almost inevitably, induce some highbrow breast-beating lament along “Whither British theatre?” lines. Yet not every production needs to be Robert Icke-style groundbreaking or punchy new drama.

With, yes, an attempt to string them into a continuous narrative ― with mixed results, it turns out ― but largely to ape the look, feel, line readings and physical business of the original as much as possible? It is one of the greatest comedies yet made, but isn’t this theatrical conservatism of the most heinous kind?
...both the physical and verbal gags land perfectly...the performances are a triumph.

Which is not to say that Fawlty Towers: The Play isn’t entertaining. The show, directed by Caroline Jay Ranger, works because Cleese and Booth (who also played waitress Polly) understood the sitcom scenario so well: a group of ill-matched characters trapped together in purgatory for our enjoyment.

And is anyone actually here for fresh and unique? If the performances in this revamp of the Torquay hotel sitcom aren’t impersonations per se, they’re near as dammit. But they’re very good ones, and audiences who already love the material (most of them, let’s face it) will not be disappointed.
Directed at a spirited lick by Caroline Jay Ranger on a split-level 70s period set, with theme-music intact, it’s wall to wall nostalgia and copper-bottomed mirth.
...efficient and energetic stage adaptation, but it's an oddly soulless affair.
..a natural for the stage: each episode is essentially a drawing-room farce...
This is theatrical time travel of the most joyful variety.
...it takes Fawlty-world on to the boards and gives it live, three-dimensional flesh.
The Play reminds us that farce works best on the stage
...lends itself particularly well to the stage seeing as it is fundamentally a farce.

Adapting a much loved television comedy series for the stage is a risky business. Theatre versions of Only Fools and Horses, Some Mothers Do ‘Ave ‘Em and Drop The Dead Donkey have met with varying degrees of success. But when you take the greatest comedy series in British Television history you take your life in your hands.
